utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, you want to make an application to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may, very briefly, Your Honours. The Prosecution, as indicated yesterday or the day before, intends to file a motion to admit exhibits from the bar table, as you put it. The motion would have to address issues of admissibility in respect to a variety of documents along a series of documents, and therefore would be in excess of the 3.000-word limit. The awkward part of the motion is that we are not sure yet, because we are working hard to try to get the motion ready tomorrow. Exactly how many words there will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't--

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We're not sure how many we would need to exceed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you need trouble yourself on this matter, because you obviously could put in several motions each of the same length, short of the 3.000, so I don't think that you should worry about that. It's a matter of convenience to put it all in the one, but the length of the motion will not matter; it's the quality that counts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you have permission to exceed the word limit. We, I don't think, have seen anything yet in relation to Mr. Coo that we anticipated receiving yesterday. Perhaps it's on its way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I believe it was sent yesterday. It should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'll see it later, no doubt. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The next witness is K82, but I see Mr. Ivetic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise, just a quick matter for clarification. It's my understanding that although the Prosecution sought reconsideration of the order that the Trial Chamber made its own initiative to initially exclude this witness's testimony and that was reversed. It's my understanding that the sanction that was imposed against the Prosecution for lack of disclosure with respect to the reference of the special police unit, the PJP, of the 18th of September 2006 is still in effect, and the latest 65 ter summary that we received just -- well, it looks like yesterday - I thought it was the day before, but in any event, recently - now has even more of a reference to the special police units. I don't know whether it's a typo or what, but all of a sudden in the first page of the 65 ter witness notification it says, soldiers including special units of the police took part in the operation, and the witness's statement does not say that, so I'm just asking for clarification whether it's a typo and indeed whether the sanction for lack of disclosure and notice continues to be in effect, as I believe it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the sanction Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That there was no reference to -- excluded from consideration any reference to the PJP in paragraph 31 of the statement, which was the only place the PJP was mentioned where the witness had said he thought he saw the PJP on the road, which was, of course, the first mention to the PJP that we had received at all. The 2002 original statement that had been disclosed to us said that there was only one policeman who was a -- from a local village who was showing them the way and did not mention the police at all. And indeed the only reference in the 2006 statement was paragraph 31 which is -- had been disclosed just days before the witness was to testify in September of 2006. And that's -- as far as I know, that's still the only reference to the PJP. That's why I'm a little bit baffled by the amended 65 ter summary that all of a sudden has -- has something different that's never been in any of the 65 ter summaries to date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph of the 65 ter summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's the first page, the very last paragraph, that begins: "In February 1999," and it begins on the end of the second line: "About 700 or 800 soldiers including special units of the police took part in the operation ..." Now, the witness's statement says military police. If that's what we're talking about, then obviously that's the clarification I need, but I obviously need to know, because I'm concerned that it could be something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Firstly, my understanding is that this 65 ter summary is identical to the one that was received previously. If the issue is in respect to the matters at Jeskovo village in paragraph 6 of the statement, which we intend to tender, then the facts stated in the statement is what we propose to lead in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did this statement exist before when the witness previously gave evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was paragraph 6 there at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were you bearing in mind the issue of paragraph 31 or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 31 also is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we are going to have to leave the bench to look at this. It's a great pity that this wasn't raised with us before we got here this morning, Mr. Ivetic. This is very unfortunate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm here in the morning with plenty of time when I come in to look at issues like this, and I can't remember the order that was made at the time. I'll need to go now and look at it and look at this issue in relation to it. We can't just sit around here flittering our way through the proceedings. Someone will speak to you so you can give them the appropriate documents and we'll have a look at them. We'll need to leave the bench for the moment to do that. --- Break taken at 9.10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I was not particularly conscious of this issue in dealing with the motion for reconsideration; on the other hand, a colleague of mine was and assumed it was implicit in our decision that the evidence in paragraph 31 would be admissible. We are months on. The issue of notice is quite different from what it was at that time. So we'll hear any further submissions that you wish to make on this point before making a final decision, since there is some doubt about the Trial Chamber's final position on it at the time the reconsideration motion was granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, reconsideration was never sought for this order in the Prosecution's motion on this matter, so I don't think it can be covered by the reconsideration. Second, with respect to notice, I respectfully submit we're at the same stages that we were in September of 2006, because since this witness was excluded and since the order was in place barring any reference to the PJP, our team would have no need to conduct any investigations with respect to this witness and this particular crime scene that was not in the indictment and with reference to the police being barred, there were no investigations conducted. We had other things to conduct. As Your Honour knows, we've been dealing with the Prosecution's case and scrambling trying to prepare our own case. So really there is no way that we could investigate within the short time-period, since this witness has been put back on our plates, more than was originally in this statement in 2002, which clearly in the statement from 2002 he says there was only one policeman with us from the village of Novak who was a local guide who showed us the terrain. So that was all we were ever put on notice for, all that we ever prepared for, and based upon that, we didn't view this witness as being a critical witness for the police and there wouldn't be much material to cross-examine him on. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp tells us that paragraph 6 was always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was in the 2006 statement given I believe two days before the witness was called to testify in September. I believe the date's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's plainly covered by the reconsideration decision. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to see. I think we're talking about two different incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, they are two different incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're talking about -- Trnje is the one that I believe I am concerned about, not Jeskovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you did raise --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then that was my mistake, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My reference to the PJP that was the subject of and is referenced at paragraph 2 of the March 13th -- the procedural history on the March 13th decision by the Trial Chamber on the reconsideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, if we decide to allow this evidence to be heard, what remedy might you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously additional time to prepare. I don't know to what extent I would be able to perform investigations at this point, but that would be -- that would be all that would be available to me, I think, at the time. I can't think of anything else I would be able to ask for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp, do you want to say anything on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think this clearly a matter of notice. That was what was indicated in the order, and I must confess that I have to find the oral order, but it was a real issue at the time. There was an issue of notice in respect to paragraph 31 where the reference was made to the PJP. But that issue -- time has passed and the Defence has received is, in my submission, adequate notice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The trouble is they had no reason to follow it up, because the witness had been excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- the decision or the indication that the witness might be re-called I think was raised -- I can't recall the date, but I think it's at least two weeks or three weeks ago. So there has been some time for the Defence to look into that. And one can look at the paragraph itself. It is part of the witness's narrative as to what he understood based on what he heard. What value can be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I say another thing in reference to paragraph 6. Although the reference to police is not in the statement itself but is in the notification, this is the same notification that was filed in September last year and this is a part of the transcript of the witness's evidence in Milosevic case. So there was adequate notice -- more than adequate notice, in respect to that part of his statement. I don't know if you need a reference to the police in the Milosevic transcript, but it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, there's no issue over paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We consider that the situation we are dealing with is quite different from the one in September, and it's clear from the reconsideration of the decision there were a number of issues -- or a number of points in issue then which are no longer a problem. We have decided that it's appropriate to hear this evidence and we think it unrealistic to exclude the particular part in paragraph 31 that's referred to. We think that Mr. Stamp has adequately answered the issue of notice; however, if it does emerge at some stage that there are points that might be clarified in the light of a short adjournment for the purpose of further inquiry, then obviously we will consider an application to provide that remedy to any accused adversely affected by this decision. We can now proceed to hear your next witness, Mr. Stamp, who is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's K82, and there are some additional protective measures in place, voice and image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, witness K82.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience while we resolved certain administrative issues here. We are now ready to proceed with your evidence. Will you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. The first person to ask you questions here will be for the Prosecution, and that will be Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, K82.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would first like to show you a document and ask you to have a look at it, that is Exhibit 2302. And can you answer me yes or no, does the particulars stated on that document relate to you personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the identification sheet which I tender be received in evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: K82, I know that you have been through some of this before, but I'm going to take you briefly through your statement again. Do you recall giving a statement to members of the Office of the Prosecution of this Tribunal on the 14th of September 2006?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And attached to that statement were certain exhibits which you marked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the statement correct and true, to the best of your knowledge and belief; that is to say, would your answers remain the same if you were asked those questions in relation to the statement again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I understand that you have had an opportunity to review again the statement and the attachments yesterday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: That is correct. I did that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the statement be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's P2315?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: K82, it's a long statement and it is before the Tribunal here, so I am not going to ask you to relate all the details that are in the statement. I wish you to assume that it has been or will be read by the Tribunal. I just want to ask you one or two questions about some aspects of the statement. At paragraph 5 of the statement you speak of a military operation which took place in Ljubizda Has in December 1998, and you said that you were ordered by Lieutenant-Colonel Konjikovac, who was the deputy of the brigade commander Delic, to return to the village in the evening and to expel the people from their houses. How do you know --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How did you become aware that Colonel Konjikovac made this order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Because during the course of the day Lieutenant-Colonel Konjikovac came to us and said we had to go back to that village in the evening, spending the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. If I'm not mistaken, I see on the screen that the witness is reading from his statement, not at this very instant, but while the questions were being put to him I saw that he was reading while answering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I respond to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Umm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can remove the statement from where it is in front of me, I certainly don't need it, if he thinks I'm reading from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could -- what's the problem with the witness having his statement in front of him? He's had to verify that it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was my understanding that yesterday he had the opportunity of reviewing to see whether it was true; he confirmed that it was true. And we are now interested in -- I mean in cross-examination we are going to see what his possibility is or ability is to reproduce certain things and we are going to look at his credibility and the truthfulness of what it is that had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can ask him to answer your questions without reference to the statement, but there's no reason why the Prosecutor can't ask his questions with reference to the statement. So at this stage there's nothing wrong with that, but the witness is quite happy to lay it to the side and proceed, so hopefully everyone's happy with that arrangement. Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I am beginning to get extremely impatient about the interruptions that are taking place without foundation, in my opinion, and we've started this morning with an inappropriate way of dealing with a matter that should have been resolved before we came on the bench. Now we've got interruptions inappropriate to the witness's evidence. He's been put through a very difficult situation by the way in which his evidence has had to come before the court. He was the subject of extensive delays when he gave evidence before. So I invite counsel to be very cautious in interrupting this any further and to insure that there's solid foundation for any interruptions. Mr. Stamp, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We were speaking about what Colonel Konjikovac told you in respect to entering the village. When your unit entered the village of Ljubizda Has, do you know where he was, that is, Colonel Konjikovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where he was. I just know in the evening when he came to see us and when he told us where it was that we would be spending the night, the military police that took the people from the village to out there where we were, where we spent the night, in that village, that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we move now to February 1999, and I refer to your statement at paragraph --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- 6, you speak about operations in the village of Jeskovo. You said that you were told by commander that about 700 soldiers would be taking part in the operation and it included special units of the police. Did you actually see and observe the units that took part in the operation; and if so, could you tell us what units took part in that operation, apart from your unit of course?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, because on the previous day the colonel who was there got us together and told us what it was that we were supposed to do the next day. The next day I really saw these special units of the police that were going with us to clean up the village, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also said in respect to that operation in February 1999 that Colonel Delic, the brigade commander, issued the order to clean up the village. I'd like to know how -- or could you just tell us, please, how did you become aware that he issued the order.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Because on the previous day he got us all together and he told us where it was that we would be going the next day, that we would be going out there to clean up that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that in that village you actually saw the bodies of ten civilians -- ten persons in civilian clothes, or who were not wearing KLA uniforms, but you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: And I don't know the exact number, but it was around ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And you said that you think about 25 to 30 people were killed in that operation. Can you elaborate upon this. On what basis do you say that perhaps 25 to 30 people were killed in that operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: When this operation was over in the evening, at the place where the army had met up, I know that that is what was said, that about 25 to 30 people had been killed. And after that, I learned that perhaps about four men were killed when we had left that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to the village of Trnje.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your unit was involved in burning houses and other property in that village. Can you say how many houses in all were burned during that operation, approximately, please, if you can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly how many houses were burned, but according to what I saw and as far as I can remember, I think it was about 20 or 30 houses for sure that we came across that had been burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how many houses were in that village? Approximately what proportion of the houses in the village were burned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Now I cannot say for sure how many, but most of the houses in that village had been burned, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you indicated that there were haystacks or agricultural assets that were burned. Can you tell us about that, about how many that were burned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes. When the action started, when we entered the village, the haystacks were the first as we walked in, and that was torched straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, was it only one haystack or were there others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Several, several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At paragraph 19 of your statement you speak of the shooting of about 15 villagers, including women and children, that you participated in. About how many members of your group participated in that shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I saw that -- well, about five or six of us, as many as happened to be there at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where were the other members of your unit at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: They were there in the yard farther away from us, and there were others in front of the entrance into the yard. They were deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Apart from the approximately five soldiers who participated, did the other members of your unit become aware of the shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, probably so. Those who were watching -- I mean, most soldiers came to that gate to see what it was that had happened. Word travels fast from one unit to another, and then people probably stopped by to see what it was that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if the senior officers became aware of this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, probably so since they issued that kind of order that civilians should be shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At -- I think the next day it was, your unit -- your company returned to its base. Where were your base at that time, and we're talking about late March 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where was your unit, your company, stationed at or based at in late March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: After that operation in Trnje, the one that you were talking about, we returned to that hill where the logistics battalion was, and I belonged to it, too, where one company had stayed behind. After that, we returned to Prizren, to some school, whatever it was. It was a school. And then we stayed there for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did members of your unit discuss the events that had taken place at Trnje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, you know what? When something happens, probably every one of us talked to someone, saying what it was that had happened, why.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we call up Exhibit 1981 -- P1981, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: K82, I know you have indicated that an order such as this, a written order such as this, would not have been given directly to personnel at your level. But there are some issues in this order I'd like to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at page 3 of the order, first paragraph on that page in English. Do we have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The order states in that part: "With some forces, prevent any spill-over and pulling out of STS which is the KLA from the area of Retimlje to the general sector of Paragusa and in the village of Trnje and Lesane and then ensure that the road remains passable and that control of the territory is established." Now, Trnje and Lesane is the area where your unit was based at the time. Is that correct? Did you hear me? I just want you to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: As far as I understand, you don't really have to resort to paragraphs. As far as I know, I cannot look at it now so that the man wouldn't say that I'm reading from it. I can only tell you about what it was that had happened, what happened in the field. As for these - what are they called? - statements, exhibits, I cannot tell you anything about things like that because that kind of thing did not reach me. That kind of thing could not have reached me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, in the order it says that the -- that you should treat the loyal civilian population correctly especially fleeing refugees and people's property and you should open fire only on features used by the STS to engage you and that you are to observe the provisions of international law. Were you in the field at Trnje and Lesane that day given any order like that, to observe international law and to treat the population correctly and not to destroy their property?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, I told you about what had happened of what was going on on the ground. I really didn't know anything about any orders, nor can I tell you anything about such provisions. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Even if he was given that order, what would it matter in light of the other orders that he claimed he was given?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- it is just to give him an opportunity to comment on something which would be the subject of argument later, that -- orders which will be -- which will be presented to the Court included orders like these were not, it is the Prosecution's case, not intended to be carried out, that these orders are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate to comment in relation to this exhibit, but what's happened here would lead us to look at the exhibit for the purpose of understanding the questions and answers, but there's no way that what has happened with this witness would amount to a satisfactory manner of introducing this document as a whole. It may have been introduced already into the case for all I know, but if not, then this is a document whose authenticity, et cetera, and whose relevance would have to be established by a written filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has no knowledge of the document whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Without showing you another document, I would just like to ask you about one thing and that is Exhibit P1995 and that is a report from the brigade command in respect to events that happened in the area where your unit is supposed to have operated during that time. And in that report it indicates that the KLA had pulled out into the villages of Trnje and Lesane during the night and were routed and crushed. Now, you were in Lesane and Trnje. I just want to ask you this: Did you have any contact or battles with KLA units during the course of the operations there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did your unit in Trnje and Lesane suffer any casualties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on from those documents now and turn to paragraph 30 to 32 of your statement, in which you describe travelling back to Trnje to collect bodies and dispose of them. Firstly, do you know who authorised or ordered your unit to return to Trnje to collect the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many soldiers travelled to Trnje to collect the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact number, but I believe that we travelled in two trucks in order to collect those bodies. As far as I can remember, there is some 10 or 20 soldiers who went there to collect the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said that when you were on your way to Zur, to the hills of Zur, to bury the bodies of the women, you were joined by other soldiers who provided an additional escort. About how many soldiers went to Zur to bury the bodies, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I remember the soldiers who were sent to the place where the bodies were buried, who were keeping guard, but I can't give you their exact number. Maybe a dozen or so were involved, but I can't give you the exact number at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, if I could clarify, you said about 20 were -- 20 went to collect the bodies and maybe a dozen or so were sent to keep guard. Would that make it approximately - and I know we are -- we can't be precise - approximately 32 soldiers went to Zur to bury the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Approximately that would be the case, but I can't give you the exact number. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where's the reference to 20?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. He said 10 to 20, actually, 10 to 20 soldiers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I noted -- the answer that I noted at that stage was 10 or 12, but I see the transcript says 10 or 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that what you said, K82, that 10 -- or could you just tell us again approximately - and I know it's approximately - how many soldiers went to collect the bodies in Trnje.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I can't be sure of that. I don't know whether there was 10 or 20. I can give you an approximation. There were between 10 and 20 soldiers, and then we were joined by the security guards, by those who were keeping guards and providing security for the -- for the area. I couldn't even see all of them. I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move on to Rugovo at paragraph 34 of the statement in which you discuss being sent with your unit by the end of April to the village of Rugovo where you participated in looting the village. These were civilian trucks that were used, according to your statement. Who drove these trucks? And I'm not asking you to identify the persons by name necessarily, but the persons who drove these trucks, did they belong to any organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, the drivers were drivers -- members of the Army of Yugoslavia, our drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And these various car parts, et cetera, were loaded on to these trucks. Where did these trucks go to, do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: From the village the lorries went back as far as I can remember. We came back on those lorries to Prizren where they had originally started from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you know how the looted property was disposed of in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about the properties. I don't know what happened in Prizren, where it ended up, what happened to that property. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, K82. There are going to be questions -- further questions of you by me colleagues, but before that could I ask you -- you had indicated in a previous statement that you had been convicted of a criminal offence and sentenced to a period of four years' imprisonment. You had been convicted of robbery in 2000 -- robbery allegedly committed in 2002, and sentenced to a term of imprisonment of four years' imprisonment and that you are in the process of appealing your conviction and sentence. Can you tell us what has become of that appeal and that case? What's its status now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I was not sent to prison for four years. I just spent ten and a half months in the investigation prison, and after that period I was sent home on provisional release. And then an appeal was filed and now this case is being retried.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You indicated in your statement the reasons why you came forward a few years ago to testify about the events, the reason including the dreams you had of the people -- crime, the people that were shot, et cetera. Can you tell us about this. You told us about those reasons some time ago. Are the reasons still the same? Why do you wish to tell your -- to tell about the events that you participated in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: This is the only reason, the reasons that you have just mentioned. That's why I decided to testify in the previous case and now. I don't have any other reason to be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, K82.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And thank you very much, Your Honours. That's the end of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will follow the following order: General Lazarevic, General Pavkovic, General Lukic, General Ojdanic, Mr. Sainovic, and Mr. Milutinovic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: K82, the first counsel for the accused to cross-examine you will be Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I didn't want to try your patience, but the last question by my learned friend is a blatant example of a leading question and the witness himself confirmed this by saying, Whatever you stated, this is how I felt. In order not to aggravate the situation that occurred this morning and not to aggravate the trial chamber, I have the authority by my colleagues to tell you that I will be the only one putting questions on behalf of General Lazarevic and General Pavkovic, I will be the only one putting questions to the witness, and maybe very briefly for General Lukic. And we promise that we will finish our cross-examination very quickly, which will enable us to finish this witness's testimony by videolink today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Let me make it clear that you and I have different views of what is leading question is. A question based on the witness's statement that he has just confirmed in court this morning seeking further information is not a leading question. Anyway, proceed now with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] K82, I shall start by quoting the end of your statement and the end of the chief examination, the examination-in-chief. You have just told us that in your state you were convicted to a prison term of four years for a robbery and that this sentence was abolished and that the case is being retried. Do you have a document to that effect? Do you know why the sentence was abolished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I submitted those documents to Mr. Barney Kelly, the investigator of the Tribunal. I believe that he has all these papers, all these documents. I was sentenced to four years in prison, and then after an appeal was filed by my lawyer, the sentence was abolished and it is being retried.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. K82, I promised the Trial Chamber that we will finish your testimony today. Could you please answer my questions briefly and can you focus on my questions. You provided Barney Kelly with certain documents that we did receive, and you provided him with these documents in 2005 or 2006. My question to you is this: In the meantime have you received any other documents? You've told us that an appeal was lodged. Do you have a document testifying to the fact that the sentence has been abolished and that it is being retried?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, that case is being retried. I have this decision and I can provide you with this document. This document is currently in the hands of my lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know why the sentence was abolished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I really don't know. Everything is stated in the decision. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you move freely about in your country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you have a passport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Why don't you have a passport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: For the aforementioned reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The reason being --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: The reason being that I was convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. How did you arrive in the place where you are now? But don't mention the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I used my ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's now go back to the event that my learned friend Stamp asked you about and also in your statement there are -- there is information about that, but you also provided a separate statement about the particular event, the act, for which you were sentenced to four years in prison. The robbery was committed on the 4th of June, 2002. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I believe so. I can't remember the date, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the 6th and 7th August, 2002, you provided your first statement to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember the date, so I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I have your first statement in front of me, and it bears the dates of 6th and 7th August, 2002.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I suppose that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you remember where the statement was provided?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this statement was provided?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know whether I'm allowed to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the Trial Chamber to move into private session just for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] K --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: K82, before you provided your first statement, did the Montenegrin police look for you on account of the robbery that was committed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And if I jog your memory and tell you that at the Milosevic trial to a question put to you by the Prosecutor as to whether there was any reason for which you were not in possession of a passport you said that there was a reason and that was the fact that you hadn't gone to the police to apply for one because some two months before that the police came to your house and your brother told you that you were being looked for. And then you turned to your relative to deal with that problem. Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: K82, your examination-in-chief took place on the 6th of September, 2002, and if you were being searched two months before that, that was in July 2002, you were being searched for this robbery some months before you provided your first statement to the Prosecution and before anybody - yourself included - knew that you would be testifying in The Hague. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: You are right, but I don't see why you are telling me all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: K82, we will be the judges of that. We are the ones who know the reasons. I'm just asking you to answer my questions. When the police looked for you, at the time you were not even a potential witness in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: That's right. I was not a potential witness. I didn't know why I was being looked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to ask the Trial Chamber if we could go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: May I conclude from your answer that you personally did not shoot at these 15 people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- can't understand this. I don't know how could you conclude that on the basis of my answer that I did not open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you shoot or did you not shoot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did shoot. Absolutely. It would not be true to say what you have just said. It is not true that I had shot at that woman and the child and it is not true that I told somebody that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But what is the truth? Who did you shoot at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I really don't know. I opened fire at the group of people in front of me. Whether I hit somebody or not, I don't know. I was just waiting for all this to end, for us to go away from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In other words, you opened fire at random without aiming at anybody specifically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you received that order from whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: From my sergeant, who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that an order that might constitute a crime is not something that you are duty-bound to carry out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. On the contrary, I was told that if you turn down -- if you refuse an order in the state of war, you may be liable to criminal responsibility, you may even receive a death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is that what you told -- they told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: We didn't do things because we wanted to do them but because we were ordered to do them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Before shooting at the group of 16 people, is it true that you mentioned that before that, you had attended an incident when your sergeant ordered a soldier --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe we have to go into private session again for the next few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second until we get into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note that the loud-speakers are on in the place where the witness is sitting and we can hear ourselves. Could the registrar over there be warned about that and could the loud-speakers be turned off because we can hear ourselves on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That will be attended to. Please continue, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I proceed? Are we still dealing with the technical problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: K82, you have just told us that you shot at random at a group of people and that you were only waiting to leave the place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How could you then count the people in that group? How could you be positive that there were 15 people in the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I did not count them. Before that, while all this was happening in the yard, I believe that there were between 10 and 15 people. I can't be sure of the exact number. I don't know whether there were exactly 15 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you opened fire at them, were they standing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No, they were sitting down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your statement and in the Milosevic case you stated that when you shot at them they fell down on top of each other. How is that possible? Now you are telling us that they were sitting down.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really don't know what else could happen. Even if a man is sitting down, he can just fall on the floor. How else could I have expressed that? How else could I have described what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your statement you say that you opened fire at random and that your only concern was to get away from there as soon as possible, and in the statement you also say that they were asked questions about the KLA, that they were asked for money, and what question -- who asked them those questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: You're trying to confuse me. This happened before the shooting started where they were being gathered in the yard, while they were being ordered to sit down. This is when all those questions were put to them, and not once -- the things happened the way I described they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And who was it who asked them all these questions about the KLA and the money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: One of the soldiers who were standing over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was that soldier from Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. In what language did he ask them all this? What was the language of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I believe that this was our language, the only that he could understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That he could understand. And then you noticed that these people as well spoke our language, the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: He did not ask all of them. He just asked one of them that he took away from the rest of the group. He did not address the entire group so that we could hear it. He took that person a little bit further away from the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's move on. It was only in your statement provided in 2006 that you said that after this incident which you attended as one of the four, five soldiers that participated in the event, that the other soldiers were so stressed out that their noses were bleeding and that they had to be hospitalised. You remember that in 2006?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who were the soldiers who were taken to the hospital, all of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No, not all four of them. Only one of them who was there. He was taken to the hospital because he was bleeding profusely and I know that he had to be taken to the hospital for the bleeding to be stopped there. It was just incredible how profusely a person could bleed from his nose. I'd never seen such a thing before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you knew why he was bleeding so heavily; this is at least what you stated in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Your Honours, I really didn't establish any diagnosis. We all believed that it was the result of stress. What else could have been at stake at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well then. Let's move on. In paragraph 11 of your statement you say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I will kindly ask the Trial Chamber to move into private session because I'm going to mention a few names.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In paragraph 13, you said that before you entered into the village the anti-aircraft gun positioned on the hill shelled the village for about 20 minutes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then the entrance into the village you came across an elderly man who was carrying cattle feed, and when he saw you he fled, jumped across the wire fence, and a burst of gun-fire was fired at him by your sergeant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: That's not true. We surrounded the village, the outskirts of the village when the anti-aircraft gun started shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then on the edge of the village you noticed this man who was carrying cattle feed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Excellent. The anti-aircraft gun is shelling the village for 20 minutes. All that time this man is carrying cattle feed as a matter of course, and when he sees you he starts running away and you kill him. So he did not hear the shelling, he did not see the shelling, and once he saw you, he got scared, he started running away, you killed him. That is your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few minutes ago I said that he is not right what he said. I said that we took up positions around the village before the anti-aircraft guns started shooting, so at that moment when we took these positions that's when that happened. It's only afterwards that the anti-aircraft gun started firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you took up positions in the village and then you were shelled by your own gun. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: At the outskirts of the village, that is where we took up positions. That is the upper position. I cannot explain it to you right now. It's underneath the gun where we had started out from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Oh, actually you were where it is that you set out from. That's what you're ultimately testifying now as opposed to what you said before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: It's not any different. That is what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You also testified that you went further on to the village of Mamusa and that over there you shelled and torched the first seven or eight houses. I am putting it to you that you invented this as well because Mamusa was a Turkish village where there was no KLA presence and where the villagers were not against the regular authorities. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I really don't know how much I agree, but as for the meadow that was there we went to the first seven or eight houses. Now, whether these houses belonged to Mamusa or not, I really cannot say anything for sure. But those first seven or eight houses were shelled and torched. After that we returned to the place where our people were firing at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: These seven or eight houses for which you say now that you don't even know whether that's Mamusa or not, how far away were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Well, I cannot know now exactly after all this time exactly. Well, it had to be at least 4 to 500 metres across this meadow I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. And now we are coming to the end of this incident. How long did the action last? If I understand your statement well, then the action took three days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Two or three days, maybe three days, I don't know, because we spent two nights there, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: After the end of this action on the fourth day you returned to collect the bodies. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was on the fourth, fifth or what day, how much later we went back to collect the bodies I can't say that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well then. Then I'll skip my next question because you're not sure of the facts there. According to your evidence when you arrived to collect the bodies, in the house where there were approximately 10 to 15 people you did not find any bodies. The only bodies that you found were the bodies of how many women and where were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: The bodies were not in the house, they were in the yard of the house, but we did not find them; that's true. As for the women's bodies, we found those on a meadow, meadow near the creek where the people had been gathered. So while they were fleeing the village they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So by the creek and the bridge across that creek. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How many women were there when you came to collect the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know, maybe four or five pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your first statement you said seven to eight women.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I can't remember. Maybe they had -- there were seven to eight, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you don't know, there might have been ten or four or five, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: There was some men and four or five women; that would be that. There were other male bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And when you arrived, they were all in the same place, the four to five men -- women and some four men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No, they were not in the same place. The men were at the same place from which the women and the children had been released. The men were gunned there and the women were shot in the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And those women were by the creek?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: They were in the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I don't know who's lying here, maybe it's you, because Witness K54 in the transcript says that when you arrived to collect the bodies that two women were in the yard, one woman was by the house, and the last two woman were in the field behind the house. He didn't mention any creeks. He didn't say that they were all together, and he was speaking about the same event when you came to collect the body. Who's telling us the truth, you or him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: When I arrived there -- I'm telling you what I saw. In the meadow there might have been -- I don't know how many women but I know there were women across the meadow, and in the creek there were the men who had been executed and the women and children had been released from there originally, and this is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you're claiming that somebody had arrived before you to collect the bodies from the yard. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I suppose so because the bodies were not there when we arrived. I don't know who we heard it from, but it seems that the special police units had collected the bodies but I can't be sure of that. We only heard that from somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's move on. And when you arrived, you collected only the female bodies and you left the male bodies lying around for somebody else to come and collect them. Do I understand your testimony well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: You understand it well, but I didn't know if anybody else would arrive. Our task was to collect the female bodies, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In paragraph 30 of your statement when you talk about your arrival for this duty to collect the female bodies, you say that on the way there you came by an elderly man with a cane, that one of the soldiers fired a single shot, and that the old man fell on the ground. Then your sergeant asked, Why did you shoot him? The soldier replied, Because you ordered me to do that. And your sergeant said to him that he should not have killed the old man before they had a chance to ask him for directions to Trnje. Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You were in Trnje for three days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But you don't know how to get to Trnje. What is a lie here? What is fabricated? Did you fabricate the whole episode? Were you at all in Trnje? Is that true or is it true that you only collected the bodies? What is the fact and what is the fabrication?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. Which question would you like the witness to answer? There's at least six there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you know where Trnje was or did you not know where Trnje was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: May I answer, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we went to Trnje, it was dark or it was very early in the morning and we took a totally different route across the villages of Novaci or whatever they're called and when we went to collect the bodies we took a main road leading to Suva Reka. So we didn't know exactly where the road forked off to Trnje, our sergeant didn't know that where we had to take the turning towards Trnje. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Earlier today on your examination-in-chief you said to my learned friend, Stamp, that there were a number of civilian lorries involved. In your statement you say that there was just one civilian lorry and a military lorry. Which is the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I apologise, what event are you asking me about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on a second. Can you clarify --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's what I was about to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you clarify that, please, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will. I have no noted it down when my learned friend, Stamp, was leading the question. He asked him whether they took civilian transportation to collect the bodies, then the answer said: "Yes." And he said that the civilian lorries were driven by soldiers. I'm putting to the witness now that in his statement he said there was just one civilian lorry and one military lorry and I am asking him what is the truth of the two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the Prosecutor asked me was about another detail, not about the event when the bodies were collected and taken away. This is when we did take civilian lorries. He didn't ask me about this other thing. I'm sure that he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question about -- or at least the answer about civilian lorries I think was in relation to paragraph 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, the events at Rogovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's certainly how I've noted it at the time, and the witness said the drivers were from the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I accept that I have misunderstood this detail. I apologise for wasting your time on this, but I have another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How many lorries did you take to collect the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but as far as I can remember, there were two lorries. But I'm not a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And those were military lorries, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I believe that one of them wasn't a military lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who did that other lorry belong to, do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't. I really don't -- how should I have known?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did it have any markings on it? What was the colour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that it had a tarpaulin, this lorry where the bodies were loaded on to. I really don't know how the lorry was marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So the lorry had tarpaulin and that was the civilian lorry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just briefly, I'm going to move on to the incident in Jeskovo and I will complete my cross-examination before the next break hopefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the first part of your statement, which refers to the action in Ljubizda Has. Did this take place in December 1998, this action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was, but I can't remember the exact dates. I really can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about dates. I'm asking you whether this was in December 1998.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I put it to you that another witness from your battalion says that this action took place on the 28th of February, who would be telling the truth, you or him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I repeat once again, I can't be sure of the period. I don't know exactly when the action took place. I really can't tell you this. I can't even know whether this was in December or in February. I know that there was a lot of snow, that I remember for a fact, but I can't remember when the action took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well, Sir. You don't have to worry about that. We are testing your credibility, your memory, and everything else here. Let's move on –

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just one second. Your question -- and you're lucky I didn't interrupt. I thought I had interrupted enough but now I will. "Who would be telling the truth you or him?" was the question. It was a question of credibility, and it's no surprise you get the answer you got?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's a mistake in the transcript. I did say that this is a question to test the witness's credibility. So there is a mistake in the interpretation and in the transcript, but in any case, I don't want to test your patience any further. I shall move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, certainly without the "not," the statement doesn't really make any sense, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Tell me, Ljubizda Has, how far is it from the border with Albania, do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know. How should I know? It may be on the border itself or at a certain distance, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. So when you say that you passed through the village and that you took some positions outside of the village, at the foot of a mountain, would you agree with me that those positions were on the border, in the border belt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know. We took up positions in the village in order to prevent anybody from descending from the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the border?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't tell you that. I don't know whether it was on the border or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. You don't know. That's okay. Let's move on. The operation Jeskovo in February 1999. You say February 1999, and I believe that you were shown documents speaking about an action that took place on the 11th of March, 1999. Where -- when was this action, in February or in March?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Again, I can't give you the exact date, I really can't. I don't know. I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know, and with the previous witness we have provided certain documents and we don't want to waste any more time and show the documents to you, do you know that this action was monitored by OSCE monitors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know that the monitors reported in their report that seven days prior to that action that the complete village was abandoned by all the civilians and there were no civilians in the village. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I only know what our commander had told us. He told us that there were no civilians there --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we can't have everybody talking at the same time. What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It appeared that counsel is referring to some event on the 11th of March on the -- it seems an assumption that a document was put to the witness about some event on the 11th of March. I don't know who put that document to the witness, so we need to know precisely about what event we are talking about. The witness has spoken about a variety of events, so if he is going to refer now to some report by some organisation, we need to identify what time, what event we are speaking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you say there that the witness had been shown documents about the 11th of March. What documents are these?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to avoid wasting time because we have recently had a witness speaking about the same developments, and then the exhibits were 5D112, 5D113, and 5D114. All these exhibits, the Chamber is aware of that, contained details that I am putting to this witness without wasting any more time. I didn't want to call up these documents in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We understood that. But earlier you did actually say that the witness had been shown these documents, and that's the point that's causing the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at page 69, line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I know exactly what you're referring to. I was referring to some other documents and I might have made a mistake. I was referring to some other documents about this action, not the OSCE documents. But he allows for the possibility that that action did take place on the 11th of March, that's why I decided to move on to the other evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you also aware of the fact that the OSCE mission verified this action, that it carried out inspection together with the Serbian MUP, and that nine members of the KLA in uniforms were found? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I've already answered that this is not something that I know. I don't know anything about the documents, about verification, or anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. But please be more concise. In the previous case, when you testified in transcript page 9859, 21/23, in contrast to your statement, you said that you had seen some ten people in civilian clothes, and then when you were asked to elaborate on that, in transcript on page 9859, lines 18 to 20, you said that when you say -- when somebody says "uniform" you mean a military uniform. And since your statement has also been entered as an exhibit, that means that in Jeskovo you saw uniformed members of KLA who had been killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I am absolutely baffled. I don't understand your question at all. What are you talking about? What uniform? Without uniform? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The men that you say you saw in this action in Jeskovo, you saw them killed in Jeskovo, you say around ten of them. Were these men in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: They were wearing clothes; but that they were wearing clothes that were the uniform of some army, that I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the suggested contradiction here, Mr. Bakrac? I didn't understand the question, either. Where is it you say the witness has referred to uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when he was asked about this incident in Jeskovo and about these ten dead persons he saw in Jeskovo, in the direct examination by Mr. Ryneveld during the Milosevic trial, and the page is 9859, lines 21 and 23, this witness said: "These persons were in civilian uniforms." When the cross-examination was over, Mr. Ryneveld --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- tried to clarify the matter with the witness, and on page 9859, lines 18 to 20, he says the following: "Yes. They were wearing civilian uniforms, ordinary uniforms."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that -- I don't know exactly what language you may have used in Serbian to address that question, but the translation in English was "civilian clothes," which makes the whole question meaningless. Now I will ask the witness the question. You're being asked what you meant in the Milosevic trial when you referred to these people as wearing civilian uniforms. Can you explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the clothing was the kind of normal clothing that a person wears, that is to say clothes that do not resemble a military uniform. As I could see these people, they were wearing everyday clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The report of the mission that these bodies were in black KLA overalls, you're not telling the truth, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I am saying what it was that I saw. I don't know what you mean by these uniforms. What are you expecting me to say? What kind of uniforms? I don't understand this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. My last question and I hope that you will be pleased to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 you said that the order for cleaning up this village of Jeskovo was given by Colonel Delic a day before you carried out this operation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How do you know about that, that he gave that kind of order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I know because we, the march class, were gathered together by him and he said that to us, that on the next day the clean-up of Jeskovo would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So the brigade commander, Colonel Delic, is now side-stepping all of his subordinates and he is issuing an order to you, the march class, that the next day you would go for this clean-up. Is that what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K82
utterances.text: I'm not saying anything. I am saying that he rallied us together and told us where it was that we were going on the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Excellent.
